Mollicelline K, which is targeted by Triptersinin A, is known to inhibit Cyanovirin-N, indicating a possible inhibitory relationship between these two compounds. This suggests that Triptersinin A may modulate the activity of G2/mitotic-specific cyclin B1, which in turn could affect the function of Mollicelline K, potentially leading to the inhibition of Cyanovirin-N. The evidence supports a pathway where Triptersinin A influences the expression or activity of cyclin B1, which then impacts the activity of Mollicelline K, thereby affecting Cyanovirin-N. The integration of these targets implies a possible regulatory or inhibitory mechanism, though the exact nature of the interaction remains to be fully elucidated.
